//: Turns the free text of a GitHub profile's Location field into a point on the homepage map. Read by tools/contributors.mjs, which prints every location it cannot find here so this file can be extended.
//places: Keys are normalised: lowercased, trimmed, one space after each comma. Several keys may share a label — that is how aliases work. A null value means the value is known not to be a place, and is skipped without a warning. A string value is an alias for another key: the entry it names is used, so the coordinates live in one place.

places.//cities: One dot each on the map, keyed by the city name on its own. Coordinates are the city centre to two decimals — the map is 1000 units wide for the whole world, where a hundredth of a degree is far under a pixel, so more precision than that is decoration. Only a handful of these have a hand-placed entry under `labels` below; the rest take the default until they actually appear on the map and their label is seen to collide with something.
places.//country-level: Some profiles name only a country. `countryOnly` marks these as a fallback: the mark sits near the country's centre and is labelled with no more than the profile said, but it is dropped entirely once a city in that country is on the map — a blob over China beside five Chinese cities reads as a sixth city nobody lives in. Dropped from the map only; the people it stood for still count toward their region in the summary, since their country is known and only their position is not. So the lat/lng here are used only while that country has no cities.
places.//aliases: The other spellings the same places arrive as: with the country or the state appended, abbreviated, in the local script, or named after the wider area rather than the city. Each is the key of the entry it stands for.
places.//not-places: Real values from real profiles that no map can place.

//regions: What the summary beside the map counts by. Continent-coarse on purpose: the UN subregions would have split the six countries the map started with into six rows, which is the country list again under another name — and the table is now long enough that subregions would be a column of ones. Every country named above appears here, so the summary never has to guess; tools/contributors.mjs warns about any that does not. Russia and Turkey straddle two continents and are each filed under one, since a country is one row or none.
//labels: Where each city's name is drawn relative to its dot, in viewBox units, keyed by label so aliases share one entry. Hand-placed because no automatic rule survives the two crowded corners of the map. Guangzhou and Shenzhen are 100km apart, which is 2.6 units at this scale, so one name goes below its dot and the other to the right; and Dublin, Cambridge, Amsterdam, Berlin and Minsk sit within 94 units of each other on one latitude, where 340 units of names have to be stacked onto separate rows above and below, with Barcelona taking the row under Amsterdam. Poland and Minsk extend that cluster east to Moscow, and on the default anchor each name ran over the next dot along — Poland's over Minsk's, Minsk's over Moscow's. So the names over the cluster are a stack, each centred on its own dot: Amsterdam on top, London and Berlin under it, Poland lowest; and Minsk's goes below its dot, into the gap above Romania. Centring is the point of it: a name that starts at its dot and runs right covers the dot after it, which read as that city's name rather than its own. Lucknow and Chengdu are the third case, and what collides there is a name with a dot rather than a name with a name: they are 64 units apart on nearly one latitude, and Chengdu's name reaches 49 of those units back west, so on the default anchor Lucknow's own name ran east under Chengdu's and Chengdu's ran over Lucknow's dot. Lucknow is anchored `end` so its name goes west into the empty Arabian Sea instead, where the nearest dot is Bengaluru's 35 units below, and Chengdu's `dy` lifts it a row above Lucknow's dot — which is the half of this that only moving Lucknow's name could not fix, since it was Chengdu's name that was sitting on somebody else's dot. A name also has to stay inside the map, which is what the eastern edge asks for: the svg does not clip, and on the default `start` anchor New Zealand's name ran 65 units past the map's right edge and into the region list beside it, so it is anchored `end` and drawn below Melbourne's row instead.
